paragraphs: Cotula cinerea Essential Oil: Chemical Composition
Compound names and reported relative percentages
Essential Oil Name

Cotula cinerea essential oil, obtained from the aerial parts of the plant. The study compares samples collected from two geographical locations (El Alamein and the Red Sea) using two extraction methods: conventional hydrodistillation (HD) and microwave-assisted hydrodistillation (MAE).
Chemical Compounds and Percentages
The table below reproduces the compound percentages reported in the supplied paper excerpt. Values are shown in the following order: El Alamein–HD, El Alamein–MAE, Red Sea–HD, and Red Sea–MAE.
Major Chemical Groups
Main Compounds
Pinocarvone was the most abundant reported compound (43.88–62.05%), followed by α-thujone (6.62–31.67%), camphene (7.07–13.49%), santolina triene (2.68–8.08%), and α-pinene (2.35–4.86%).
Notes on the Data

• The percentages are the relative composition values reported for each sample in the supplied paper excerpt; they should not automatically be interpreted as exact weight percentages.
• A value of 0.00 means the compound was reported as zero/not detected in that sample under the study's analysis; it does not necessarily prove absolute absence.
• These are four sample profiles of the same essential oil, not four different essential oils.
Source

Ali, S. K., Saleh, I. A., El-Gendy, A. E.-N. G., Abd El Aty, A. A., Mohamed, T. A., & Hegazy, M.-E. F. “Effect of Geographical Location and Extraction Methods on the Chemical Composition and Antimicrobial Activity of Cotula cinerea Essential Oil via Chemo-Metric Analysis.” PMCID: PMC13453069; PMID: 42571628.
Note: The source details above are limited to the bibliographic information included in the supplied text.
Volatile Composition of Egyptian Hedychium coronarium and Alpinia zerumbet

This document summarizes the volatile compounds and relative peak-area percentages reported in Table 1 of the supplied article. The study examined two plant species, two plant parts (leaves and rhizomes), and two extraction methods (hydrodistillation and headspace).
Number of Oils and Compounds
Plant species studied: 2 — Hedychium coronarium and Alpinia zerumbet.
Oil/volatile profiles compared: 8 profiles — leaf and rhizome samples for each species, each analyzed using hydrodistillation (HD) and headspace (HS).

Compound counts reported in the abstract/results: H. coronarium leaves: 47 (HD) and 16 (HS); H. coronarium rhizomes: 39 (HD) and 15 (HS); A. zerumbet leaves: 19 (HD) and 21 (HS); A. zerumbet rhizomes: 23 (HD) and 16 (HS).

These counts add up to 196 compound detections across the eight profiles, not 196 unique chemical compounds. The article's Table 1 contains a combined list of compounds across samples; compounds can occur in more than one profile.

Important Data Notes
Percentages are relative GC/MS peak-area percentages, as reported in Table 1; they are not necessarily weight percentages of the oil.
A dash in the original table indicates that a compound was not reported for that sample. Compounds absent from a profile have not been listed in that profile.

The article's abstract and discussion provide compound counts for the eight profiles. Some cells in the pasted Table 1 appear blank or difficult to interpret in text extraction, so the lists above transcribe the visible non-dash percentages from the supplied text. Please check against the original table/PDF before formal publication.

The study includes two plant species cultivated and collected in Egypt: Hedychium coronarium and Alpinia zerumbet. It compares eight plant-part/extraction-method profiles, not eight different plant species.
Reference

Shahat, E. A., Ayoub, I. M., Bakr, R. O., Gad, H. A., Eldahshan, O. A., & Singab, A. N. B. (2026). Comparative analysis of volatile composition and anticholinesterase activity of Egyptian Hedychium coronarium and Alpinia zerumbet using chemometric assessment of extraction techniques. Scientific Reports, 16, 15209. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-51750-1
Lavender Essential Oils — GC–MS Data Extraction
Data extracted from a Scientific Reports (2026) study of four commercial lavender oils in the Egyptian market.
Important Notes Before Using the Data
Oil name: Lavender essential oil.
Scientific plant name: The Methods section identifies the samples as Lavandula angustifolia Mill.; the paper also uses the broader term Lavandula spp. in its title/introduction.

Plant part: The paper states that lavender essential oil is generally obtained by steam distillation from flowers and leaves. However, it does not specify which plant part was used for each of the four commercial products.
Therefore, the plant part for each individual commercial sample cannot be assigned specifically as flowers or leaves based on the information reported in this study.
Percentages are mean relative GC–MS peak-area percentages, with standard deviation (SD) where reported. They should not automatically be interpreted as absolute mass concentrations such as mg/g.
A dash (–) indicates that no value was reported for that compound in the published table for that sample; it does not necessarily prove absolute absence.
Both individual compound values and chemical-class totals are included. A chemical-class total must not be treated as the percentage of a single compound.
Extracted Data
Product codes used in the study: L-Nef (Nefertari), L-Imt (Imtenan), L-Sha (Shana), and L-Rag (Ragab).
Key Findings from the Study
L-Sha had the highest Linalool percentage among the samples (33.61% ± 0.26) and the highest Linalyl acetate percentage (46.09% ± 0.30).
L-Rag contained Linalool at 24.72% ± 1.88 and Linalyl acetate at 32.65% ± 2.37.
L-Nef contained 2,4-Pentanediol at 16.21% ± 2.60, which the paper discusses as atypical for the expected lavender-oil profile.

L-Imt had a reported total fatty acid/ester class value of 24.39% ± 25.00 and Oleyl acetate at 12.08% ± 20.92. The authors discuss possible carrier oils or formulation additives, but these findings alone do not conclusively prove adulteration.
Study Reference
"Comparative metabolite profiling of commercial lavender oils in the Egyptian market using GC–MS and chemometric analysis." Scientific Reports (2026).
Article: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-45972-6
Database Recommendation

For computational use, keep separate fields for product name, scientific plant name, plant part, compound name, percentage, SD, value type (individual compound or compound-group total), and source. Do not guess the plant part for a product if the study does not report it.

paragraphs: Melaleuca quinquenervia Leaf Essential Oil
Chemical Composition: Identified Compounds, Relative Abundance, and Chemical Classes
1. Essential Oil and Botanical Source
Essential oil: Melaleuca quinquenervia Leaf Essential Oil (MQLEO)
Botanical source: Melaleuca quinquenervia (Cav.) S.T. Blake
Plant part: Leaves
Collection location reported in the paper: Shanbari, Oseem, Giza, Egypt
Collection period: January 2025
Extraction method: Hydrodistillation using a Clevenger apparatus
Chemical profiling method: Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC/MS)
2. Identified Chemical Constituents

The study reports 19 identified constituents. The percentages below are relative GC/MS peak-area percentages (Area %), as reported in Table 1; they should not automatically be interpreted as exact weight percentages.
3. Major Chemical Group Percentages
Note on the total: the article’s Results prose reports 98.09%, whereas Table 1 reports 98.05%. The group summary above follows the Table 1 total and percentages.
4. Original Research Paper

Fikry, E.; Orfali, R.; Perveen, S.; Ghaffar, S.; El-Shafae, A. M.; El-Domiaty, M. M.; Tawfeek, N. Chemical Composition and Anti-Lung Cancer Activities of Melaleuca quinquenervia Leaf Essential Oil: Integrating Gas Chromatography–Mass Spectrometry (GC/MS) Profiling, Network Pharmacology, and Molecular Docking. Pharmaceuticals (Basel). 2025 May 22; 18(6):771. doi:10.3390/ph18060771.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/ph18060771
Full-text article: https://www.mdpi.com/1424-8247/18/6/771
5. Important Interpretation Note

This document summarizes the chemical-composition data reported in the cited paper. The reported relative abundance can vary with plant origin, growing conditions, extraction procedures, and analytical methods. The paper’s chemical profile refers specifically to the Egyptian leaf essential oil analyzed in this study.
Chemical Composition of Pimenta racemosa Leaf Essential Oil
Plant species: Pimenta racemosa (Mill.) J. W. Moore
Plant part: Leaves
Collection location: El-Zohrya Garden, Zamalek, Cairo Governorate, Egypt
Total identified composition: 99.76% of the oil, according to Table 1.
Identified Chemical Compounds and Relative Percentages
Major Chemical Classes Reported in the Article
Important Notes
This article reports one essential oil: the leaf essential oil of Pimenta racemosa collected in Egypt.

Table 1 lists 17 compounds, with a total identified composition of 99.76%. However, the abstract says that fourteen compounds were detected. This is an internal inconsistency in the supplied article text; this document follows the detailed Results section and Table 1, which list 17 compounds.
The percentages are relative GC-MS peak-area percentages, not necessarily weight percentages of the entire oil.

The plant species is described in the article as native to Venezuela, Puerto Rico, and Jamaica; the studied leaves were grown/collected in Egypt. Therefore, it is more accurate to call this an essential oil extracted from a plant grown in Egypt, rather than a species native only to Egypt.
Reference

Eldahshan, O. A., Nilofar, N., Zengin, G., & El-Nashar, H. A. S. “Chemical profile of essential oil from Pimenta racemosa leaves, antioxidant potential, and its enzyme inhibitory properties.” Scientific Reports (2025). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-15542-3. PMCID: PMC12371097.

Corrected transcription of Table 3: GC–MS analysis of control and salt-affected plants

Source: Soliman, M. M., Elsaba, Y. M., Soliman, M. S. A., & Ahmed, E. Z. (2024). “Composition and antimicrobial activity of Rosmarinus officinalis L. and Artemisia monosperma L. leaf essential oils and methanolic extracts from plants grown in normal and saline habitats in Egypt.” Scientific Reports, 14, Article 7342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-57301-w
How to read the table

RT = retention time as reported in the article. Control % and Salt % are the reported relative composition values for essential oils from control plants and salt-affected plants, respectively. A dash (—) means that the compound was not reported/detected in that condition in Table 3. These GC–MS percentages represent relative composition and should not automatically be interpreted as weight percentages of the whole oil.
A. Rosmarinus officinalis L. (Rosemary) Essential Oil
B. Artemisia monosperma L. Essential Oil
Verification notes and discrepancies
The numerical values in the tables above follow the Table 3 transcription supplied in the conversation and were checked against the article page.

The article's Results prose conflicts with Table 3 for rosemary α-pinene: the prose says 15.52% in control plants, while Table 3 lists 17.52%. This document uses the Table 3 value (17.52%) because the requested source is Table 3.
The article's Results prose gives salt-stressed rosemary verbenone as 26.15%, while Table 3 lists 26.1%. This document uses the Table 3 value (26.1%).
Some compound-class labels are blank or unusual in the supplied table. They have been retained as reported or marked 'Not specified in supplied table' rather than silently reclassified.
A dash (—) has been used consistently for entries shown as a dash in the supplied Table 3.
Article link
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-57301-w
Salvia fruticosa Essential Oil
Identified chemical compounds and reported percentages
Essential Oil Name

Salvia fruticosa essential oil (EO), extracted from the aerial parts of the plant. The study compared three extraction approaches: hydrodistillation (HD), headspace (HS), and supercritical fluid extraction (SF).
Chemical Composition
Percentages below are reproduced from Table 1 of the supplied article. A dash (—) indicates that the compound was not detected/reported for that extraction method in the table.
Summary of Reported Composition
Main Compounds Reported

Hydrodistillation (HD): Eucalyptol (43.87%) and camphor (9.99%) were the most abundant reported compounds.
Headspace (HS): Eucalyptol (35.67%), α-thujene (24.88%), (-)-α-pinene (9.66%), and camphene (8.77%) were the major reported compounds.
Supercritical fluid extraction (SF): Iso-caryophyllene (17.07%), 13-epi-manoyl oxide (12.52%), α-guaiene (5.08%), and viridiflorol (5.62%) were among the main reported compounds.
Source Reference

Hashad, N., Sary, H. G., Khazaal, M. T., & Moharram, F. A. (2026). Impact of extraction method on the chemical composition and antibacterial potential of Salvia fruticosa essential oil. BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies, 26, 165. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12906-026-05376-5. PMID: 42067804; PMCID: PMC13135703.

Abbreviations: HD = hydrodistillation; HS = headspace; SF = supercritical fluid extraction. The compound percentages are reported values from the article's Table 1 and should not automatically be interpreted as exact weight percentages.
